blocks.title: What ICAI's published papers tell us
bullets: ICAI has published no examiners' comments for Paper 6; the guidance below comes from its suggested answers, RTPs and MTPs.
**This is the most reliably examined chapter in Section A.** A ratio question has appeared in Q1 of every past paper from May 2024 to May 2026, and in every RTP and every MTP in the set.

The dominant form is **reverse working**: you are given ratios and asked to build the Balance Sheet, the Trading and Profit & Loss Account, or a missing figure. Ten of the thirty-three official questions here are of that type.
The second form is **compute and comment**: calculate five named ratios from a given set of figures (Jan 2026, May 2025, Sep 2025, May 2024).
Two-mark parts test the **effect of a transaction on a ratio** (Jan 2026 asked whether the current ratio improves, declines or stays unchanged).

blocks.title: How ICAI marks this chapter (study guidance)
bullets: Marks are for the **formula, the working note and the answer** — in that order. A correct number with no working rarely gets full marks; a correct formula with an arithmetic slip usually keeps most of them.
Always **state the formula before substituting**. ICAI's own answers do this every time.

Where the study material allows more than one formula (debt-equity, ROCE), ICAI accepts either — but says: 'ratios shall be calculated based on requirement and availability of information', and **if you deviate, state your assumption**.
The numerator must correspond to the denominator: cost of goods sold with average inventory, credit sales with average receivables, credit purchases with average payables.

concepts.title: 1–2. Introduction, Ratio and Ratio Analysis, and the Sources of Financial Data
understand: **Why ratios at all (§1).** The basis for financial analysis, planning and decision making is the **financial statements**, which mainly consist of the **Balance Sheet and the Profit and Loss Account**. The profit and loss account shows the **operating activities of the concern over a period of time**; the balance sheet depicts the **balance value of the acquired assets and of liabilities**, i.e. the **financial position of an organisation at a particular point of time**.

However, these statements **do not disclose all of the necessary and relevant information**. To obtain the material and relevant information necessary for **ascertaining the financial strengths and weaknesses** of an enterprise, the data depicted in the financial statement has to be analysed. The financial manager has analytical tools for this; **one of the main tools is ratio analysis**.

**Definition of a ratio (§2.1).** ==A ratio is defined as **"the indicated quotient of two mathematical expressions and as the relationship between two or more things"**.== Here, ratio means **financial ratio or accounting ratio, which is a mathematical expression of the relationship between two accounting figures**.

**Ratio analysis (§2.2).** The term financial ratio is explained by how it is calculated and what the objective of the calculation is. **Basis of calculation:** a relationship **expressed in mathematical terms**, **between two individual figures or groups of figures**, **connected with each other in some logical manner**, **selected from the financial statements of the concern**. **Objective:** so that all stakeholders — owners, investors, lenders, employees and others — can draw conclusions about the **performance (past, present and future)** and the **strengths and weaknesses of a firm**, and **can take decisions in relation to the firm**.

==Ratio analysis rests on the fact that **a single accounting figure by itself may not communicate any meaningful information, but when expressed relative to some other figure it may provide significant information**.==

Ratio analysis is **not just comparing different numbers** from the balance sheet, income statement and cash flow statement. It is comparing the number against **previous years (intra-firm comparison)**, against **other companies (inter-firm comparison)**, against the **industry**, or even against **the economy in general**.

**Sources of financial data for analysis (§2.3)** — six sources: **(i) annual reports, (ii) interim financial statements, (iii) notes to accounts, (iv) statement of cash flows, (v) business periodicals, (vi) credit and investment advisory services**.
concepts.example: A profit of ₹50 lakh means nothing on its own. Against sales of ₹10 crore it is a 5% net profit ratio; against capital employed of ₹2 crore it is a 25% return. The second figure is what gives the first its meaning.

concepts.title: 3–3.1 Types of Ratios and the Liquidity Ratios
concepts.evidence: PYQ 1 (Jan 2026 Q4(c) OR) · MTP 1 (Sep 2024 Series I)
understand: **Four families (§3).** Ratios are classified as **liquidity ratios (short-term solvency)**; **leverage ratios (long-term solvency)**, split into **capital structure ratios and coverage ratios**; **activity ratios (also called efficiency, performance or turnover ratios)**; and **profitability ratios**, split into those **related to sales**, those **related to overall return on investment (assets, capital employed, equity)**, those **required for analysis from the owner's point of view**, and those **related to market, valuation and investors**. The study material adds a footnote: ==**liquidity ratios should be examined taking the relevant turnover ratios into consideration**.==

**Liquidity (§3.1).** The terms **'liquidity' and 'short-term solvency' are used synonymously**: the **ability of the business to pay its short-term liabilities**. Inability affects **credibility as well as credit rating**; continuous default leads to **commercial bankruptcy**, which may lead to **sickness and dissolution**. Short-term lenders and creditors are very interested in the state of liquidity because of their financial stake. ==**Both lack of sufficient liquidity and excess liquidity is bad for the organisation.**==

**(a) Current ratio** = **Current Assets ÷ Current Liabilities**. It is **one of the best known measures of short-term solvency** and the most common measure of short-term liquidity. The question it addresses: *does the business have enough current assets to meet the payment schedule of its current debts with a margin of safety for possible losses in current assets?* **Current assets** = inventories + sundry debtors + cash and bank balances + receivables/accruals + loans and advances + disposable investments + any other current assets. **Current liabilities** = creditors for goods and services + short-term loans + bank overdraft + cash credit + outstanding expenses + provision for taxation + proposed dividend + unclaimed dividend + any other current liabilities. ==A **generally acceptable current ratio is 2:1**, but whether a specific ratio is satisfactory depends on the **nature of the business and the characteristics of its current assets and liabilities**.==

**(b) Quick ratio or acid-test ratio** = **Quick Assets ÷ Current Liabilities**, where ==**Quick Assets = Current Assets − Inventories − Prepaid expenses**==. It is a **much more conservative measure** than the current ratio and answers: *if all sales revenues should disappear, could the business meet its current obligations with the readily convertible quick funds on hand?* Inventories are deducted on the belief that they are **not near-cash assets** and because **in times of financial difficulty inventory may be saleable only at liquidation value** — though **in a seller's market inventories are also near-cash assets**. ==An **acid-test of 1:1 is considered satisfactory** unless the majority of quick assets are in accounts receivable and the pattern of collection lags behind the schedule for paying current liabilities.==

**(c) Cash ratio or absolute liquidity ratio** = **(Cash and Bank balances + Marketable Securities) ÷ Current Liabilities**, or **(Cash and Bank balances + Current Investments) ÷ Current Liabilities**. It **measures the absolute liquidity of the business** and **tests short-term liquidity only in terms of cash and marketable securities or current investments**.

**(d) Basic defense interval or interval measure** = **(Cash and Bank balances + Net Receivables + Marketable Securities) ÷ (Operating Expenses ÷ number of days, say 360)**, or **(Current Assets − Prepaid expenses − Inventories) ÷ Daily Operating Expenses**, where **daily operating expenses = (cost of goods sold + selling, administration and other general expenses − depreciation and other non-cash expenditure) ÷ number of days in a year**. ==If all the company's revenues were suddenly to cease, this ratio tells you **the number of days for which the company can cover its cash expenses without additional financing**.==

**(e) Net working capital** = **Current Assets − Current Liabilities (excluding short-term bank borrowing)**. It is **more a measure of cash flow than a ratio**; the result **must be a positive number**, though in certain business models it may be negative. **Bankers look at net working capital over time** to judge a company's **ability to weather financial crises**, and **loans are often tied to minimum working capital requirements**.
concepts.example: Current assets ₹8,00,000 and current liabilities ₹3,20,000 give a current ratio of 2.5. If inventory is ₹3,20,000, quick assets are ₹4,80,000 and the quick ratio is 1.5 — comfortably above the 1:1 benchmark.

official_questions.question: BEE Ltd. has a current ratio of 2:1, showing enough short-term liquidity. Comment whether the current ratio will improve, decline or remain unchanged after each of the following: (i) a debtor owing ₹60,000 becomes insolvent and only 75% is recovered in cash in full and final settlement; (ii) equity shares are issued for ₹2,00,000, the proceeds kept in the current account with the bank; (iii) ₹25,000 is collected from customers in cash; (iv) goods costing ₹8,000 are sold for ₹12,500 on credit.
answer_points: **(i) Declines.** The write-off of 25% of a ₹60,000 debtor reduces current assets by ₹15,000 with no change in current liabilities.
**(ii) Improves.** Current assets rise by the ₹2,00,000 kept in the bank while current liabilities are unchanged.
**(iii) No change.** One current asset (debtors) simply becomes another current asset (cash); the total is unchanged.
**(iv) Improves.** Stock of ₹8,000 is replaced by debtors of ₹12,500, so current assets rise by the ₹4,500 profit.
official_questions.conclusion: Half a mark each; give the direction first and the one-line reason after.
official_questions.examiner: No examiners' comments have been published for Paper 6.

official_questions.question: Calculate the total current assets of Ananya Limited from: stock turnover 5 times; sales (all credit) ₹7,20,000; gross profit ratio 25%; current liabilities ₹2,40,000; liquidity ratio 1.25. Stock at the end is ₹30,000 more than stock in the beginning.
answer_points: **Step 1 — Cost of goods sold.** Gross profit ratio 25% on sales of ₹7,20,000 gives **cost of goods sold = 75% of ₹7,20,000 = ₹5,40,000**.

**Step 2 — Average and closing stock.** Stock turnover 5 times gives **average stock = ₹5,40,000 ÷ 5 = ₹1,08,000**. Since closing stock is ₹30,000 more than opening stock, opening + ₹30,000 = closing and their average is ₹1,08,000, so **opening stock = ₹93,000 and closing stock = ₹1,23,000**.
**Step 3 — Liquid assets.** SM §3.1(b): liquidity ratio = Liquid assets ÷ Current liabilities, so **liquid assets = 1.25 × ₹2,40,000 = ₹3,00,000**.
**Step 4 — Total current assets.** **Current assets = Liquid assets + Closing stock = ₹3,00,000 + ₹1,23,000 = ₹4,23,000.**
The current ratio here works out to ₹4,23,000 ÷ ₹2,40,000 = 1.76 : 1, below the study material's generally acceptable 2 : 1 — a comment worth adding if the question asks for one.
official_questions.conclusion: Four short steps; the average-stock reconciliation is the only place to slip.

expected_questions.question: A company has current assets of ₹8,00,000, of which inventories are ₹3,20,000 and prepaid expenses ₹40,000. Cash and bank balances are ₹1,20,000 and marketable securities ₹40,000. Current liabilities are ₹3,20,000, which include a bank overdraft of ₹60,000. Annual operating expenses are ₹14,40,000 (including depreciation of ₹1,44,000). Assume a 360-day year. Compute the current ratio, the quick ratio, the cash ratio, the basic defense interval and net working capital, and comment.
answer_points: **Current ratio** = Current assets ÷ Current liabilities = ₹8,00,000 ÷ ₹3,20,000 = **2.5 : 1**, above the generally acceptable 2:1.

**Quick ratio** = (Current assets − Inventories − Prepaid expenses) ÷ Current liabilities = (₹8,00,000 − ₹3,20,000 − ₹40,000) ÷ ₹3,20,000 = ₹4,40,000 ÷ ₹3,20,000 = **1.375 : 1**, above the satisfactory 1:1.
**Cash ratio** = (Cash and bank balances + Marketable securities) ÷ Current liabilities = (₹1,20,000 + ₹40,000) ÷ ₹3,20,000 = **0.5 : 1**.

**Basic defense interval** = (Current assets − Prepaid expenses − Inventories) ÷ Daily operating expenses. Daily operating expenses = (₹14,40,000 − ₹1,44,000) ÷ 360 = ₹3,600. So ₹4,40,000 ÷ ₹3,600 = **122 days (approx.)** of cash expenses covered without additional financing.

**Net working capital** = Current assets − Current liabilities excluding short-term bank borrowing = ₹8,00,000 − (₹3,20,000 − ₹60,000) = **₹5,40,000**, a positive figure, which bankers read as the ability to weather a financial crisis.
Comment: liquidity is comfortable on every measure; the study material cautions that excess liquidity is as unwelcome as a shortage, so the turnover ratios should be read alongside.

mcqs.question: VP Ltd. provides the following information: Current Ratio 1.5:1; Sales (80% credit sales) ₹150 lakh; Inventory Turnover Ratio 6 times; Average Collection Period 2 months; Gross Profit Ratio 20%; Quick Ratio 1:1. Inventory and Receivables would be:
mcqs.explanation: **Inventory:** gross profit is 20% of sales, so COGS = 80% × ₹150 lakh = **₹120 lakh**. Inventory turnover (on COGS) is 6 times, so Inventory = 120 ÷ 6 = **₹20 lakh**. **Receivables:** credit sales = 80% × ₹150 lakh = **₹120 lakh**; with an average collection period of 2 months, Receivables = 120 × 2/12 = **₹20 lakh**. ICAI key: (A).

why_wrong.B: ₹10 lakh each would follow from using a 12-times turnover and a 1-month collection period.
why_wrong.C: This takes inventory on a 12-times turnover while getting receivables right.
why_wrong.D: This reverses the receivables figure, as if the collection period applied to one month.

mcqs.trap: Two traps in one item. Inventory turnover here is computed **on cost of goods sold**, not on sales, so the gross profit ratio must be used first. And the collection period applies to **credit sales only** — 80% of ₹150 lakh, not the whole ₹150 lakh. Here both errors happen to cancel in the receivables figure, which is why the examiner also asks part 7.

mcqs.question: Continuing with VP Ltd. (Current Ratio 1.5:1, Quick Ratio 1:1, Inventory ₹20 lakh), Current Assets and Current Liabilities would be:
mcqs.explanation: Let current liabilities be CL. Current ratio 1.5:1 gives CA = 1.5 CL; quick ratio 1:1 gives Quick Assets = 1.0 CL. Since Quick Assets = CA − Inventory, Inventory = 1.5 CL − 1.0 CL = **0.5 CL**. Inventory is ₹20 lakh from part 6, so **CL = ₹40 lakh** and **CA = 1.5 × 40 = ₹60 lakh**. ICAI key: (C).

why_wrong.A: 30 and 20 would need inventory of ₹10 lakh.
why_wrong.B: 45 and 30 would need inventory of ₹15 lakh.
why_wrong.D: 75 and 50 would need inventory of ₹25 lakh.

mcqs.trap: The whole item turns on one line: **the difference between the current ratio and the quick ratio, multiplied by current liabilities, is the inventory**. Every option is internally consistent with some other inventory figure, so a wrong answer in part 6 propagates into part 7 — which is exactly why ICAI pairs them.

mcqs.question:
**The Solstice Biotech Ltd. case (MTP Sep 2026 Series 2, Part I).** A manufacturer of diagnostic kits scaled production to a record high after a public-health screening initiative and has approached Continental Trade Bank for a working-capital and investment loan, submitting three years of statements. For 2025-26: Sales ₹16,000k, COGS ₹9,600k, PBT ₹2,400k, Interest ₹680k, PAT ₹1,680k; Cash ₹212k, Receivables ₹4,200k (opening ₹3,000k), Inventories ₹4,500k (opening ₹3,000k), Total Assets ₹18,312k; Equity Share Capital ₹4,000k, Other Equity ₹3,752k, Non-Current Borrowings ₹5,000k, Current Liabilities ₹5,560k.

Based on the FY 2025-26 figures of Solstice Biotech Ltd., what are the Current Ratio and the Acid-test (Quick) Ratio?
mcqs.explanation: **Current Assets = Cash and Cash Equivalents + Accounts Receivable + Inventories = 212 + 4,200 + 4,500 = ₹8,912k.** **Current Ratio = 8,912 ÷ 5,560 = 1.60 : 1.** **Quick Assets = Current Assets − Inventories = 8,912 − 4,500 = ₹4,412k**, so **Quick Ratio = 4,412 ÷ 5,560 = 0.79 : 1**. ICAI key: (A).

why_wrong.B: 2.30 : 1 and 1.20 : 1 are the **industry averages** given in the case, not the company's ratios.
why_wrong.C: The current ratio is right but the quick ratio has not deducted the full inventory.
why_wrong.D: 1.80 : 1 and 0.93 : 1 are the company's **2024-25** ratios, one year earlier.

mcqs.trap: Three of the four options are real numbers from the same table — the industry average and the prior year. Read which year and whose figures the question asks for before computing anything.

concepts.title: 3.2–3.2.1 Long-term Solvency: the Capital Structure Ratios
understand: **What leverage ratios do (§3.2).** ==Leverage ratios are those financial ratios which **measure the long-term stability and capital structure of the firm**.== They indicate the **mix of funds provided by owners and lenders** and assure the lenders of long-term funds with regard to **(i) periodic payment of interest during the period of the loan and (ii) repayment of the principal amount on maturity**. They are of two types: **capital structure ratios** and **coverage ratios**.

**Capital structure ratios (§3.2.1)** provide an insight into the **financing techniques used by a business** and focus on the **long-term solvency position**. From the balance sheet one gets only the absolute fund employed and its sources; **only capital structure ratios show the relative weight of different sources**.

**(a) Equity ratio = Shareholders' Equity ÷ Net Assets.** Shareholders' equity is **equity share capital and reserves and surplus (excluding fictitious assets etc.)**. **Net assets or capital employed includes net fixed assets and net current assets (current assets − current liabilities).** It indicates the **proportion of owner's fund to total fund invested**; traditionally, the **higher the proportion of owner's fund, the lower the degree of risk for potential lenders**.

**(b) Debt ratio = Total Debt ÷ Net Assets.** **Total debt or total outside liabilities includes short and long term borrowings from financial institutions, debentures or bonds, deferred payment arrangements for buying capital equipment, bank borrowings, public deposits and any other interest-bearing loan.** ==A **ratio greater than 1 would mean a greater portion of company assets are funded by debt** and could be a risky scenario.==

**(c) Debt to equity ratio = Total Outside Liabilities ÷ Shareholders' Equity**, i.e. **Total Debt ÷ Shareholders' Equity**, or **Long-term Debt ÷ Shareholders' Equity**. The study material's own footnotes: total debt is **not merely long-term debt, i.e. both current and non-current liabilities**; and **sometimes only interest-bearing long-term debt is used instead of total liabilities (exclusive of current liabilities)**. A **high** ratio means **less protection for creditors**; a **low** ratio indicates a **wider safety cushion**. It is **very often used for capital structure decisions** such as the issue of shares or debentures, and is ==**the indicator of a firm's financial leverage**==.

**(d) Debt to total assets ratio = Total Outside Liabilities ÷ Total Assets**, or **Total Debt ÷ Total Assets**. It measures the **proportion of total assets financed with debt** and therefore **the extent of financial leverage**; the **higher the ratio, the less the assets are backed up by equity and hence the higher the financial leverage**.

**(e) Capital gearing ratio** shows the **proportion of fixed interest (dividend) bearing capital to funds belonging to equity shareholders**, i.e. equity funds or net worth; again, a **higher ratio may indicate more risk**. ==**Capital Gearing Ratio = (Preference Share Capital + Debentures + Other Borrowed funds) ÷ (Equity Share Capital + Reserves & Surplus − Losses).**==

**(f) Proprietary ratio = Proprietary Fund ÷ Total Assets.** **Proprietary fund includes equity share capital, preference share capital and reserves and surplus.** **Total assets exclude fictitious assets and losses.** It indicates the **proportion of total assets financed by shareholders**; the **higher the ratio, the less risky the scenario**.
concepts.example: Equity share capital ₹8,00,000, reserves ₹2,00,000, 10% preference ₹3,00,000 and debentures ₹7,00,000 give a capital gearing ratio of (3,00,000 + 7,00,000) ÷ (8,00,000 + 2,00,000) = 1 : 1.

official_questions.question: A manufacturing company growing at a good rate has a given financial leverage; identify the related ratio figure. (ICAI's topic label for this question is 'Ratio Analysis and Leverages'.)
answer_points: The question links the **debt-equity ratio of Chapter 3 with the degree of financial leverage of Chapter 6** — the study material calls the debt-equity ratio **the indicator of the firm's financial leverage** (SM §3.2.1(c)).
The route is: the degree of financial leverage = EBIT ÷ EBT = EBIT ÷ (EBIT − interest), so a given leverage figure fixes the interest, and the interest at the stated rate fixes the debt.
With debt known and the balance sheet total or equity given, the **debt-equity ratio** follows.
This is why the study material insists that liquidity ratios be read with turnover ratios and that leverage ratios be read with profitability ratios — no ratio stands alone.
official_questions.conclusion: A one-mark MCQ that is really a two-chapter question.

concepts.title: 3.2.2 The Coverage Ratios
understand: ==Coverage ratios **measure the firm's ability to service the fixed liabilities**. They establish the relationship between **fixed claims and what is normally available out of which these claims are to be paid**.== The **fixed claims** consist of **(i) interest on loans, (ii) preference dividend, and (iii) amortisation of principal, or repayment of the instalment of loans, or redemption of preference capital on maturity**.

**(a) Debt Service Coverage Ratio (DSCR).** Lenders are interested in debt service coverage to **judge the firm's ability to pay off current interest and instalments**. ==**DSCR = Earnings available for debt services ÷ (Interest + Instalments).**== **Earnings available for debt service = Net profit (earnings after taxes) + non-cash operating expenses like depreciation and other amortisations + interest + other adjustments like loss on sale of fixed assets.** Fund from operations (or cash from operations) before interest and taxes may also be used as required. ==**Normally a DSCR of 1.5 to 2 is satisfactory.**== Sometimes **lease rentals are added to both numerator and denominator**.

**(b) Interest coverage ratio**, also known as the ==**'times interest earned ratio'**==, indicates the firm's ability to meet interest and other fixed charge obligations. ==**Interest Coverage Ratio = Earnings before interest and taxes (EBIT) ÷ Interest.**== **EBIT is used in the numerator because the ability to pay interest is not affected by the tax burden, as interest on debt funds is a deductible expense.** It measures **how many times a company can cover its current interest payment with its available earnings** and **reflects the margin of safety** for paying interest during a given period. A **high** ratio means the enterprise can **easily meet its interest obligations even if EBIT suffers a considerable decline**; a **lower** ratio indicates **excessive use of debt or inefficient operations**.

**(c) Preference dividend coverage ratio** measures the ability of a firm to pay dividend on preference shares which carry a stated rate of return. ==**Preference Dividend Coverage Ratio = Net profit or earnings after taxes (EAT) ÷ Preference dividend.**== It indicates the **margin of safety available to the preference shareholders**; a higher ratio is desirable from their point of view. Similarly, **Equity Dividend Coverage Ratio = (Earnings after taxes − Preference dividend) ÷ Equity dividend**.

**(d) Fixed charges coverage ratio** shows **how many times the cash flow before interest and taxes covers all fixed financing charges**. ==**Fixed Charges Coverage Ratio = (EBIT + Depreciation) ÷ (Interest + Repayment of Loan).**== ==A ratio of **more than 1 is considered as safe**.==

**The study material's notes for calculating ratios.** (1) **EBIT = PBIT; EAT = PAT; EBT = PBT.** (2) ==**Ratios shall be calculated based on requirement and availability of information and may deviate from the original formulae; if required, assumptions should be given.**== (3) **The numerator should be taken in correspondence with the denominator and vice versa.**
concepts.example: EAT ₹6,00,000, depreciation ₹2,00,000, interest ₹1,00,000 and instalments ₹3,00,000 give earnings available for debt service of ₹9,00,000 and a DSCR of 9,00,000 ÷ 4,00,000 = 2.25 — above the satisfactory 1.5 to 2.

expected_questions.question: A company reports earnings after tax of ₹6,00,000, depreciation ₹2,00,000, interest on a term loan ₹1,00,000, an annual loan instalment of ₹3,00,000, preference dividend ₹50,000 and equity dividend ₹1,50,000. The tax rate is 25%. Compute the debt service coverage ratio, the interest coverage ratio, the preference dividend coverage ratio, the equity dividend coverage ratio and the fixed charges coverage ratio, and comment.
answer_points: **Working note — earnings available for debt service** = EAT + non-cash operating expenses + interest = ₹6,00,000 + ₹2,00,000 + ₹1,00,000 = **₹9,00,000**. **EBIT** = EAT ÷ (1 − t) + interest = ₹6,00,000 ÷ 0.75 + ₹1,00,000 = ₹8,00,000 + ₹1,00,000 = **₹9,00,000**.
**Debt service coverage ratio** = Earnings available for debt service ÷ (Interest + Instalments) = ₹9,00,000 ÷ (₹1,00,000 + ₹3,00,000) = **2.25 times**, above the satisfactory range of 1.5 to 2.
**Interest coverage ratio** = EBIT ÷ Interest = ₹9,00,000 ÷ ₹1,00,000 = **9 times**, a wide margin of safety; EBIT can decline considerably before interest becomes difficult to pay.
**Preference dividend coverage ratio** = Earnings after taxes ÷ Preference dividend = ₹6,00,000 ÷ ₹50,000 = **12 times**.
**Equity dividend coverage ratio** = (Earnings after taxes − Preference dividend) ÷ Equity dividend = (₹6,00,000 − ₹50,000) ÷ ₹1,50,000 = **3.67 times**.

**Fixed charges coverage ratio** = (EBIT + Depreciation) ÷ (Interest + Repayment of loan) = (₹9,00,000 + ₹2,00,000) ÷ (₹1,00,000 + ₹3,00,000) = **2.75 times**, well above the 1 that the study material calls safe.

mcqs.question:
**The Solstice Biotech Ltd. case (MTP Sep 2026 Series 2, Part I).** A manufacturer of diagnostic kits scaled production to a record high after a public-health screening initiative and has approached Continental Trade Bank for a working-capital and investment loan, submitting three years of statements. For 2025-26: Sales ₹16,000k, COGS ₹9,600k, PBT ₹2,400k, Interest ₹680k, PAT ₹1,680k; Cash ₹212k, Receivables ₹4,200k (opening ₹3,000k), Inventories ₹4,500k (opening ₹3,000k), Total Assets ₹18,312k; Equity Share Capital ₹4,000k, Other Equity ₹3,752k, Non-Current Borrowings ₹5,000k, Current Liabilities ₹5,560k.

The Interest Coverage Ratio of Solstice Biotech Ltd. fell to 4.53 times in FY 2025-26 (industry average 10 times) while its Debt-to-Equity Ratio rose to 64.50% (industry average 35%). As the credit appraisal officer, what should be your primary concern in appraising this loan proposal?

options.A: Both figures are favourable, so the loan can be sanctioned without further scrutiny
options.B: The falling interest coverage combined with rising leverage signals a reduced cushion to service debt and heightened repayment risk, warranting closer scrutiny before further lending
options.C: The interest coverage ratio is irrelevant once the debt-to-equity ratio is known
options.D: Since sales are growing, both ratios can be ignored in the loan decision

mcqs.explanation: **Interest Coverage = EBIT ÷ Interest = (PBT + Interest) ÷ Interest = (2,400 + 680) ÷ 680 = 4.53 times.** ICAI's own reasoning: **'A ratio of 4.53 times, well below the industry norm of 10 times, means earnings cover interest obligations with a much thinner margin than peers. Combined with a Debt-to-Equity Ratio of 64.50% (industry average 35%), the company is both more leveraged than its peers and less able to comfortably service that debt from operating earnings. For a loan officer, this combination — rising leverage and weakening debt-servicing capacity — is the key red flag in the proposal, not a reason for automatic approval.'** ICAI key: (B).

why_wrong.A: Both figures are materially **worse** than the industry average, not favourable.
why_wrong.C: The two ratios answer different questions — leverage measures the stock of debt, coverage the capacity to service it — so neither makes the other irrelevant.
why_wrong.D: Growing sales are what caused the receivables and inventory build-up and the extra borrowing; growth is the context for the concern, not an answer to it.

mcqs.trap: This is the interpretation question the whole case builds to, and the lesson is the one the chapter's limitations section makes: a single ratio means little, and **two ratios read together** can say something neither says alone. Sales growth with falling coverage and rising leverage is the classic over-trading signature.

official_questions.question: Theme Ltd.: 12.5% debt ₹45,00,000; debt to equity ratio 1.5 : 1; return on shareholders' fund 54%; operating ratio 85%; ratio of operating expenses to cost of goods sold 2 : 6; tax rate 25%; fixed assets ₹39,00,000; current ratio 1.8 : 1. Calculate (i) the interest coverage ratio, (ii) the gross profit ratio, (iii) current assets.
answer_points: **Step 1 — Shareholders' fund and profits.** Debt to equity is 1.5 : 1 on debt of ₹45,00,000, so **shareholders' fund = ₹45,00,000 ÷ 1.5 = ₹30,00,000**. Return on shareholders' fund is 54%, so **profit after tax = 54% of ₹30,00,000 = ₹16,20,000**, and with tax at 25%, **profit before tax = ₹16,20,000 ÷ 0.75 = ₹21,60,000**.

**Step 2 — EBIT and interest coverage.** Interest = 12.5% of ₹45,00,000 = **₹5,62,500**. **EBIT = ₹21,60,000 + ₹5,62,500 = ₹27,22,500.** SM §3.2.2: **Interest coverage ratio = EBIT ÷ Interest = ₹27,22,500 ÷ ₹5,62,500 = 4.84 times.**

**Step 3 — Sales and the gross profit ratio.** The operating ratio is 85%, so operating profit (EBIT) is 15% of sales, giving **Sales = ₹27,22,500 ÷ 0.15 = ₹1,81,50,000**. Operating expenses to cost of goods sold is 2 : 6, so of the 85% operating ratio, cost of goods sold is 6/8 = **63.75% of sales** and operating expenses 2/8 = 21.25%. **Gross profit ratio = 100% − 63.75% = 36.25%.**

**Step 4 — Current assets.** Total assets = shareholders' fund + debt + current liabilities. With fixed assets of ₹39,00,000 and a current ratio of 1.8 : 1, current assets = 1.8 × current liabilities, and the balance sheet identity gives the current liabilities figure; **current assets then follow as 1.8 times that**.
The chain is: debt-equity gives shareholders' fund; return on shareholders' fund gives PAT; tax gives PBT; interest gives EBIT; the operating ratio gives sales.
official_questions.conclusion: Three requirements, but the whole answer hangs on reaching EBIT first.
official_questions.examiner: No examiners' comments have been published for Paper 6.

official_questions.question: Vardhaman Limited for the year ending 31st March 2024: current ratio 3:1; loan funds to owned funds 1:3; gross profit ratio 25%; stock turnover ratio 10; net working capital ₹5,00,000; return on total assets (pre-tax) 15%; market price per share ₹20; total assets turnover ratio 2.5; opening stock ₹6,50,500; fixed assets ₹15,00,000; 75,000 equity shares of ₹10 each; 25,000 12% preference shares of ₹10 each; depreciation ₹50,000; interest on debt 9%; future instalments ₹2,00,000; tax rate 25%. Calculate (i) quick ratio, (ii) fixed assets turnover ratio, (iii) debt service coverage, (iv) earnings per share, (v) price-earnings ratio.
answer_points: **Step 1 — Current assets and current liabilities.** Current ratio 3:1 means net working capital = 2 × current liabilities, so **current liabilities = ₹5,00,000 ÷ 2 = ₹2,50,000** and **current assets = ₹7,50,000**.

**Step 2 — Total assets and sales.** **Total assets = Fixed assets + Current assets = ₹15,00,000 + ₹7,50,000 = ₹22,50,000.** Total assets turnover 2.5, so **Sales = 2.5 × ₹22,50,000 = ₹56,25,000**; with a gross profit ratio of 25%, **cost of goods sold = ₹42,18,750**.

**Step 3 — Closing stock and the quick ratio.** Stock turnover 10 on cost of goods sold gives average stock = ₹4,21,875, so **closing stock = (2 × ₹4,21,875) − ₹6,50,500 = ₹1,93,250**. SM §3.1(b): **Quick ratio = (Current assets − stock) ÷ Current liabilities = (₹7,50,000 − ₹1,93,250) ÷ ₹2,50,000 = 2.23 : 1**.
**(ii) Fixed assets turnover ratio** = Sales ÷ Fixed assets = ₹56,25,000 ÷ ₹15,00,000 = **3.75 times**.

**Step 4 — EBIT, interest and profit.** Return on total assets (pre-tax) 15% gives **EBIT = 15% of ₹22,50,000 = ₹3,37,500**. Owned funds = total assets − current liabilities − loan funds; with loan funds to owned funds at 1:3, the loan funds follow, and **interest = 9% of loan funds**. EBT = EBIT − interest; **PAT = EBT × 0.75**.
**(iii) Debt service coverage.** SM §3.2.2: Earnings available for debt service = PAT + depreciation + interest; **DSCR = that figure ÷ (Interest + Future instalments of ₹2,00,000)**.
**(iv) EPS** = (PAT − preference dividend of 12% on ₹2,50,000 = ₹30,000) ÷ 75,000 shares. **(v) P/E ratio** = ₹20 ÷ EPS.
This single RTP question walks through four of the chapter's five families — liquidity, activity, coverage and market — which is why it is the best one to rehearse.
official_questions.conclusion: Five requirements from one data set; the opening move is current liabilities from working capital.

official_questions.question: Continuing the ABC Industries Ltd. question, the bank has raised issues on the accounts. The chief executive asks the statutory auditor to prepare a reply quoting the proper ratio for each issue, in the format: issue, ratio, numerator, denominator, ideal ratio or range, the company's ratio, and whether it is favourable or adverse. One of the issues concerns the ratio that 'shows how many times the cash flow before interest and taxes covers all fixed financing charges'. Closing fixed assets, after providing 20% depreciation, constituted 60% of total assets; current assets comprise inventories, advance tax, prepaid insurance and receivables.
answer_points: **The ratio described is the fixed charges coverage ratio** (SM Ch 3 §3.2.2): it shows how many times the cash flow before interest and taxes covers all fixed financing charges. **Numerator: EBIT + depreciation. Denominator: interest + repayment of loan.** A ratio of **more than 1 is considered safe**.

**For a liquidity issue**, quote the current ratio (current assets ÷ current liabilities, generally acceptable at 2:1) or the quick ratio (current assets less inventories and prepaid expenses ÷ current liabilities, satisfactory at 1:1). Note that **prepaid insurance must be excluded from quick assets**, which is why the question lists it separately.

**For a debt-servicing issue**, quote the debt service coverage ratio — earnings available for debt service ÷ (interest + instalments) — normally satisfactory at 1.5 to 2, or the interest coverage ratio, EBIT ÷ interest.
**For a solvency issue**, quote the debt-equity ratio or the proprietary ratio; **for an efficiency issue**, the relevant turnover ratio.

The answer format ICAI asks for is itself the lesson: every ratio has a numerator, a denominator, an ideal range where the study material gives one, and a verdict — and a ratio quoted without its ideal range answers nothing.
official_questions.conclusion: Match each issue to the ratio that measures it, and give the study material's benchmark where one exists.

concepts.title: 3.3 Activity Ratios (Efficiency, Performance or Turnover Ratios)
concepts.evidence: PYQ 2 (May 2025 Q1(a), Jan 2026 Q1(a)) · RTP 2 (Sep 2024, Sep 2026) · MTP 3 (Jan 2026 both series, Sep 2024 Series I)
understand: ==These ratios are employed to **evaluate the efficiency with which the firm manages and utilises its assets**, and for that reason are often called **'asset management ratios'**.== They usually indicate the **frequency of sales with respect to its assets** — capital assets, working capital or average inventory — and are **usually calculated with reference to sales or cost of goods sold and expressed in terms of rate or times**.

**(a) Total asset turnover ratio = Sales or Cost of Goods Sold ÷ Total Assets.** It measures the efficiency with which the firm uses its total assets; **higher the ratio, better it is**. A high ratio indicates **efficient utilisation of total assets in generation of sales**; a low ratio indicates total assets are not efficiently used.

**(b) Fixed assets turnover ratio = Sales or Cost of Goods Sold ÷ Fixed Assets.** A high ratio indicates efficient utilisation of fixed assets in generating sales. The study material's caution: ==a firm whose **plant and machinery are old may show a higher fixed assets turnover ratio** than a firm which has purchased them recently== — because the older assets carry a lower written-down value.

**(c) Capital turnover ratio or net asset turnover ratio = Sales or Cost of Goods Sold ÷ Net Assets.** Since **net assets equals capital employed**, it is also known as the capital turnover ratio. It indicates the firm's **ability to generate sales or cost of goods sold per rupee of long-term investment**; the higher the ratio, the more efficient the **utilisation of owner's and long-term creditors' funds**.

**(d) Current assets turnover ratio = Sales or Cost of Goods Sold ÷ Current Assets**, measuring the efficiency of using current assets. **(e) Working capital turnover ratio = Sales or Cost of Goods Sold ÷ Working Capital**, measuring **how effective a company is at generating sales for every rupee of working capital put to use**. The higher the ratio, the more efficient the utilisation of working capital — **however, a very high working capital turnover ratio indicates that the company needs to raise additional working capital for future needs**. Working capital turnover is further segregated into **inventory turnover, debtors turnover and creditors turnover**.

**(i) Inventory or stock turnover ratio** establishes the relationship between the **cost of goods sold during the year and the average inventory held during the year** and measures the efficiency with which a firm utilises or manages its inventory. ==**Inventory Turnover Ratio = Cost of Goods Sold (or Sales) ÷ Average Inventory**, where **Average Inventory = (Opening Stock + Closing Stock) ÷ 2**.== For raw material, ==**Raw Material Inventory Turnover Ratio = Raw Material Consumed ÷ Average Raw Material Stock**.== It indicates **how fast inventory is used or sold**: a **high ratio is good from the viewpoint of liquidity**; a low ratio would indicate that inventory is **not used, sold or lost and stays on a shelf or in the warehouse for a long time**.

**(ii) Receivables (debtors) turnover ratio.** Where a firm sells goods on credit, realisation of sales revenue is delayed and receivables are created. **The speed with which these receivables are collected affects the liquidity position of the firm.** The ratio **throws light on the collection and credit policies of the firm**. ==**Receivables Turnover Ratio = Credit Sales ÷ Average Accounts Receivable.**== A **low** debtors turnover ratio reflects **liberal credit terms granted to customers**; a **high** ratio shows that **collections are made rapidly**. ==**Receivables velocity or average collection period = Average Accounts Receivable ÷ Average Daily Credit Sales**, or **12 months / 52 weeks / 360 days ÷ Receivables Turnover Ratio**==, where **average daily credit sales = credit sales ÷ number of days in the year (say 360)**. It measures the **average number of days it takes to collect an account receivable** and is also referred to as the **number of days of receivable** or the **number of days' sales in receivables**.

**(iii) Payables turnover ratio** is calculated on the same lines and **measures how fast a company makes payment to its creditors**, showing the **velocity of payables payment**. ==**Payables Turnover Ratio = Annual Net Credit Purchases ÷ Average Accounts Payable.**== A **low** creditors turnover ratio reflects **liberal credit terms granted by suppliers**; a **high** ratio shows accounts are settled rapidly. ==**Payables velocity or average payment period = Average Accounts Payable ÷ Average Daily Credit Purchases**, or **12 months / 52 weeks / 360 days ÷ Payables Turnover Ratio**.== The firm can compare **what credit period it receives from suppliers with what it offers to customers**, and against the industry average.
==The study material notes that **inventory turnover, receivables turnover and payables turnover are also relevant to examine the liquidity of an organisation**.==

**The study material's notes for calculating these ratios.** (1) ==**Only selling and distribution expenses differentiate Cost of Goods Sold (COGS) and Cost of Sales (COS); in their absence COGS will be equal to Cost of Sales.**== (2) **Cost of goods sold or cost of sales can be used to calculate turnover ratios, eliminating the profit part.** (3) **Average total assets, fixed assets, current assets, net assets or working capital can also be taken in the denominator; in fact when average figures are available it may be preferred to use them.** (4) **Ratios shall be calculated based on requirement and availability of information and may deviate from the original formulae; if required, assumptions should be given.**

official_questions.question: From the books of AIL Limited for 2024-25: gross profit margin (25% of sales) ₹30,00,000; inventory holding period 28 days; opening inventory ₹8,00,000; current ratio 1.20; quick ratio 0.80; selling and distribution expenses ₹12,00,000; depreciation and other non-cash expenses ₹4,80,000. Assume 360 days. Calculate (i) inventory as on 31.03.2025, (ii) working capital, (iii) basic defense interval.
answer_points: **Step 1 — Sales and cost of goods sold.** Gross profit is ₹30,00,000 and is 25% of sales, so **Sales = ₹30,00,000 ÷ 0.25 = ₹1,20,00,000** and **Cost of goods sold = ₹1,20,00,000 − ₹30,00,000 = ₹90,00,000**.

**Step 2 — Average and closing inventory.** Inventory holding period 28 days means the inventory turnover ratio is 360 ÷ 28 times. Average inventory = Cost of goods sold ÷ Inventory turnover = ₹90,00,000 × 28 ÷ 360 = **₹7,00,000**. Since average inventory = (opening + closing) ÷ 2 and opening inventory is ₹8,00,000, **closing inventory = (2 × ₹7,00,000) − ₹8,00,000 = ₹6,00,000**.

**Step 3 — Working capital.** The gap between the current ratio and the quick ratio is inventory: current assets − quick assets = inventory, i.e. (1.20 − 0.80) × current liabilities = ₹6,00,000, so **current liabilities = ₹6,00,000 ÷ 0.40 = ₹15,00,000** and **current assets = 1.20 × ₹15,00,000 = ₹18,00,000**. **Working capital = ₹18,00,000 − ₹15,00,000 = ₹3,00,000.**

**Step 4 — Basic defense interval.** SM §3.1(d): (Current assets − prepaid expenses − inventories) ÷ Daily operating expenses. Liquid assets = ₹18,00,000 − ₹6,00,000 = ₹12,00,000. Daily operating expenses = (Cost of goods sold + selling and distribution expenses − depreciation and other non-cash expenses) ÷ 360 = (₹90,00,000 + ₹12,00,000 − ₹4,80,000) ÷ 360 = ₹97,20,000 ÷ 360 = ₹27,000. **Basic defense interval = ₹12,00,000 ÷ ₹27,000 = 44.44 days (approx.).**

The chain to remember: gross profit ratio gives sales and cost of goods sold; the holding period gives average and then closing inventory; the gap between the current and quick ratios gives current liabilities.
official_questions.conclusion: Three requirements, but one chain — sales, then inventory, then the two ratios, then the defense interval.

official_questions.question: Prashuk Ltd.: fixed assets turnover ratio (based on cost of sales) 8 times; capital turnover ratio (based on cost of sales) 2 times; inventory turnover 8 times; receivable turnover 4 times; payable turnover 6 times; GP ratio 25%. Gross profit for the year is ₹8,00,000. There is no long-term loan or overdraft. Reserves and surplus amount to ₹2,00,000. Ending inventory is ₹20,000 above the beginning inventory. Determine the various assets and liabilities of the company.
answer_points: **Step 1 — Sales and cost of sales.** Gross profit is 25% of sales and amounts to ₹8,00,000, so **Sales = ₹32,00,000** and **cost of sales = ₹24,00,000**.

**Step 2 — Fixed assets and capital employed.** Fixed assets turnover 8 times on cost of sales gives **fixed assets = ₹24,00,000 ÷ 8 = ₹3,00,000**. Capital turnover 2 times gives **capital employed = ₹24,00,000 ÷ 2 = ₹12,00,000**.

**Step 3 — Inventory.** Inventory turnover 8 times on cost of sales gives an **average inventory of ₹3,00,000**; since ending inventory is ₹20,000 above the beginning, **closing inventory = ₹3,10,000 and opening inventory = ₹2,90,000**.

**Step 4 — Receivables and payables.** Receivable turnover 4 times on sales gives **receivables = ₹32,00,000 ÷ 4 = ₹8,00,000**. Purchases = cost of sales − opening inventory + closing inventory = ₹24,00,000 + ₹20,000 = ₹24,20,000, so **payables = ₹24,20,000 ÷ 6 = ₹4,03,333 (approx.)**.

**Step 5 — The funding side.** With no long-term loan or overdraft, capital employed of ₹12,00,000 is share capital plus reserves and surplus of ₹2,00,000, so **share capital = ₹10,00,000**; cash is the balancing current asset.
The instruction 'based on cost of sales' appears twice here and is the marks: using sales instead would inflate both fixed assets and capital employed.
official_questions.conclusion: Five turnover ratios, five figures — each one a single division once sales and cost of sales are known.

official_questions.question: A concern reports: debtors velocity 3 months; creditors velocity 2 months; stock turnover ratio 1.5; gross profit ratio 25%; bills receivable ₹25,000; bills payable ₹10,000; gross profit ₹4,00,000; fixed assets to turnover ratio 4. Closing stock is ₹10,000 above the opening stock. Calculate (i) sales and cost of goods sold, (ii) sundry debtors, (iii) sundry creditors, (iv) closing stock, (v) fixed assets.
answer_points: **(i) Sales and cost of goods sold.** Gross profit is 25% of sales and is ₹4,00,000, so **Sales = ₹16,00,000** and **Cost of goods sold = ₹12,00,000**.

**(ii) Sundry debtors.** Debtors velocity 3 months gives total receivables = ₹16,00,000 × 3 ÷ 12 = ₹4,00,000. Bills receivable of ₹25,000 form part of that, so **sundry debtors = ₹4,00,000 − ₹25,000 = ₹3,75,000**.

**(iii) Sundry creditors.** Purchases = Cost of goods sold + increase in stock = ₹12,00,000 + ₹10,000 = ₹12,10,000. Creditors velocity 2 months gives total payables = ₹12,10,000 × 2 ÷ 12 = ₹2,01,667, and deducting bills payable of ₹10,000 leaves **sundry creditors = ₹1,91,667 (approx.)**.

**(iv) Closing stock.** Stock turnover 1.5 on cost of goods sold gives an average stock of ₹12,00,000 ÷ 1.5 = ₹8,00,000; with closing ₹10,000 above opening, **closing stock = ₹8,05,000** and opening stock = ₹7,95,000.
**(v) Fixed assets.** Fixed assets to turnover ratio 4 gives **fixed assets = ₹16,00,000 ÷ 4 = ₹4,00,000**.

The two traps: bills receivable and bills payable must be **deducted** from the total to reach sundry debtors and sundry creditors, and purchases, not cost of goods sold, drive the creditors velocity.
official_questions.conclusion: Five requirements; the bills receivable and bills payable adjustments are where marks are lost.

expected_questions.question: A company reports sales of ₹48,00,000 (all on credit), a gross profit ratio of 25%, opening stock ₹2,50,000, closing stock ₹3,50,000, opening debtors ₹5,50,000, closing debtors ₹6,50,000, opening creditors ₹3,00,000 and closing creditors ₹3,60,000. All purchases are on credit. Assume a 360-day year. Compute the inventory turnover ratio, the receivables turnover ratio and collection period, and the payables turnover ratio and payment period.
answer_points: **Working note 1 — Cost of goods sold** = Sales − Gross profit = ₹48,00,000 − 25% of ₹48,00,000 = **₹36,00,000**.
**Working note 2 — Purchases** = Cost of goods sold − Opening stock + Closing stock = ₹36,00,000 − ₹2,50,000 + ₹3,50,000 = **₹37,00,000**.

**Inventory turnover ratio** = Cost of goods sold ÷ Average inventory = ₹36,00,000 ÷ [(₹2,50,000 + ₹3,50,000) ÷ 2] = ₹36,00,000 ÷ ₹3,00,000 = **12 times**; inventory holding period = 360 ÷ 12 = **30 days**.

**Receivables turnover ratio** = Credit sales ÷ Average accounts receivable = ₹48,00,000 ÷ [(₹5,50,000 + ₹6,50,000) ÷ 2] = ₹48,00,000 ÷ ₹6,00,000 = **8 times**; average collection period = 360 ÷ 8 = **45 days**.

**Payables turnover ratio** = Annual net credit purchases ÷ Average accounts payable = ₹37,00,000 ÷ [(₹3,00,000 + ₹3,60,000) ÷ 2] = ₹37,00,000 ÷ ₹3,30,000 = **11.21 times**; average payment period = 360 ÷ 11.21 = **32 days (approx.)**.
Comment: the firm collects in 45 days but pays in 32, so it funds a 13-day gap plus 30 days of stock out of its own working capital.

concepts.title: 3.4–3.4.1 Profitability Ratios and those Based on Sales
concepts.evidence: PYQ 1 (May 2024 Q1(a)) · MTP 2 (Mar 2024 Series II, Sep 2025 Series II)
understand: ==**Profitability ratios measure the profitability or the operational efficiency of the firm**; they **reflect the final results of business operations** and are **some of the most closely watched and widely quoted ratios**. Management attempts to maximise them **to maximise the firm's value**.==

Results can be evaluated **with reference to a given level of assets, or sales, or owner's interest**, so profitability ratios fall into **four categories: (i) related to sales, (ii) related to overall return on investment, (iii) required for analysis from the owner's point of view, (iv) related to market, valuation and investors**.

**(a) Gross profit ratio or gross profit margin** ==**= (Gross Profit × 100) ÷ Sales**==. It **measures the percentage of each sale in rupees remaining after payment for the goods sold**. It **depends on the relationship between sales price, volume and costs**, and a **high gross profit margin is a favourable sign of good management**.

**(b) Net profit ratio or net profit margin** measures the relationship between net profit and sales. Depending on the concept of net profit: ==**Net Profit Ratio = (Net Profit × 100) ÷ Sales**, or **(Earnings after taxes × 100) ÷ Sales**; and **Pre-tax Profit Ratio = (Earnings before taxes × 100) ÷ Sales**.== It finds **the proportion of revenue that finds its way into profits after meeting all expenses**; a high ratio indicates positive returns from the business.

**(c) Operating profit ratio** is calculated to evaluate the **operating performance** of the business. ==**Operating Profit Ratio = (Operating Profit × 100) ÷ Sales**, or **(EBIT × 100) ÷ Sales**, where **Operating Profit = Sales − Cost of Goods Sold − Operating Expenses**.== It measures **the percentage of each sale in rupees that remains after payment of all costs and expenses except interest and taxes**. It is **followed closely by analysts because it focuses on operating results**, and **operating profit is often referred to as earnings before interest and taxes**.

**(d) Expenses ratios**, in four variants: ==**Cost of Goods Sold Ratio = (COGS × 100) ÷ Sales**; **Operating Expenses Ratio = [(Administrative expenses + Selling and Distribution overheads) × 100] ÷ Sales**; **Operating Ratio = [(COGS + Operating expenses) × 100] ÷ Sales**; **Financial Expenses Ratio = (Financial expenses × 100) ÷ Sales**==, where financial expenses **exclude taxes, loss due to theft, goods destroyed by fire and the like**. **Administration expenses ratio and selling and distribution expenses ratio can be calculated in similar ways.**
concepts.example: Sales ₹50,00,000, cost of goods sold ₹35,00,000 and operating expenses ₹7,50,000 give a gross profit ratio of 30%, an operating ratio of 85% and an operating profit ratio of 15%. Operating ratio and operating profit ratio always add to 100%.

concepts.title: 3.4.2 Profitability Ratios Related to Overall Return on Assets or Investments
concepts.evidence: PYQ 1 (Sep 2025 Q1(b)) · RTP 2 (Jan 2026 Du Pont, Sep 2026) · MTP 2 (Mar 2024 Series II, May 2026 Series I)
understand: ==**Return on Investment (ROI) is the most important ratio of all.** It is the **percentage of return on funds invested in the business by its owners** and tells the owner **whether or not all the effort put into the business has been worthwhile**.== ==**ROI = (Return or Profit or Earnings × 100) ÷ Investment**, which can be split as **(Return ÷ Sales) × (Sales ÷ Investment) = Profitability Ratio × Investment Turnover Ratio**.== So ==**ROI can be improved either by improving the profitability ratio, or the investment turnover ratio, or both**.==

Investment may be **total assets or net assets**; **funds employed in net assets are also known as capital employed, which is net worth plus debt**, where **net worth is the equity shareholders' fund**. The three broad categories are **Return on Assets (ROA) — including Return on Total Assets (ROTA) and Return on Net Assets (RONA) — Return on Capital Employed (ROCE), and Return on Equity (ROE)**.

**(i) Return on Assets (ROA)** measures profitability **in terms of assets employed to earn that profit**. ==**ROA = Net Profit after taxes ÷ Average Total Assets** (or Average Tangible Assets, or Average Fixed Assets)==; sometimes **total assets may be used instead of average assets**. Here net profit is exclusive of interest; because **assets are also financed by lenders**, ROA can also be computed as ==**(Net Profit after taxes + Interest) ÷ Average Total/Tangible/Fixed Assets**, or **EBIT(1 − t) ÷ Average Total Assets** — known as **Return on Total Assets (ROTA)** — or **EBIT(1 − t) ÷ Average Net Assets** — known as **Return on Net Assets (RONA)**.==

**(ii) Return on Capital Employed (ROCE)**, another variation of ROI: ==**ROCE (Pre-tax) = (EBIT × 100) ÷ Capital Employed**; **ROCE (Post-tax) = [EBIT(1 − t) × 100] ÷ Capital Employed**==; sometimes also **[(Net Profit after taxes + Interest) × 100] ÷ Capital Employed**. ==**Capital Employed = Total Assets − Current Liabilities**, or **Fixed Assets + Working Capital**, or **Equity + Long Term Debt**.== ==**ROCE should always be higher than the rate at which the company borrows.**== **Intangible assets** (goodwill, patents, trade marks) **should be included in capital employed**, but **no fictitious asset (such as deferred expenses) should be included**. If information is available, **average capital employed shall be taken**.

**(iii) Return on Equity (ROE)** measures the profitability of equity funds invested in the firm and **reveals how profitably the owners' funds have been utilised**. ==**ROE = [(Net Profit after taxes − Preference dividend, if any) ÷ Net Worth or Equity Shareholders' Funds] × 100.**== It is **one of the most important indicators of a firm's profitability and potential growth**: companies with a high ROE and little or no debt **can grow without large capital expenditures**. The study material's caution: **two companies can have the same return on equity, yet one can be a much better business**. If **return on total shareholders** is calculated, **net profit after taxes before preference dividend is divided by the total shareholders' fund including preference share capital**.

**The Du Pont model.** A finance executive at E.I. Du Pont de Nemours and Co. created the DuPont system of financial analysis in **1919**. Its three components are the **net profit margin, the asset turnover and the equity multiplier**. **(i) Profitability or net profit margin = Profit or Net Income ÷ Sales or Revenue** — the after-tax profit per rupee of revenue; it varies across industries, and **it is not uncommon for management purposely to lower the net profit margin in a bid to attract higher sales**. The study material calls the margin **a safety cushion: the lower the margin, the less room for an error** — a business with a 1% margin **has no room for flawed execution**. **(ii) Investment turnover, asset turnover or capital turnover = Sales or Revenue ÷ Investment, Assets or Capital** — how effectively a company converts its assets into sales; it **tends to be inversely related to the net profit margin**. **(iii) Equity multiplier = Investment, Assets or Capital ÷ Shareholders' Equity** — a **measure of financial leverage** that **allows the investor to see what portion of the return on equity is the result of debt**, since **a company with terrible sales and margins can take on excessive debt and artificially increase its return on equity**.

==**Return on Equity = Net Profit Margin × Asset Turnover × Equity Multiplier.**== The study material's worked example: revenue ₹29,261, net income ₹4,212, assets ₹27,987 and shareholders' equity ₹13,572 give a net profit margin of **14.39%**, an asset turnover of **1.0455** and an equity multiplier of **2.0621**, so ROE = 0.1439 × 1.0455 × 2.0621 = **31.02%**. Leaving out the equity multiplier shows what the company would earn if it were completely debt-free: ROE drops to **15.04%** (0.1439 × 1.0455). So **15.04% of the return on equity was due to profit margins and sales, while the remaining 15.98% was due to returns earned on the debt at work in the business** — and a company at a comparable valuation with the same ROE but a higher internally generated portion **would be more attractive**.

concepts.title: 3.4.3 Profitability Ratios from the Owner's Point of View
understand: **(a) Earnings per Share (EPS).** The profitability of a firm **from the point of view of ordinary shareholders** can be measured on an earnings per share basis. ==**EPS = Net profit available to equity shareholders ÷ Number of equity shares outstanding.**== The study material's note: **in the absence of preference dividend, profit after tax can be taken as earnings available to equity shareholders.**

**(b) Dividend per Share (DPS).** Earnings per share reflects the profitability of a firm per share, but **it does not reflect how much profit is paid as dividend and how much is retained by the business**. Dividend per share indicates **the amount of profit distributed to equity shareholders per share**. ==**DPS = Total Dividend paid to equity shareholders ÷ Number of equity shares outstanding.**==

**(c) Dividend Pay-out Ratio (DP).** This ratio **measures the dividend paid in relation to net earnings** and is determined **to see to what extent earnings per share have been retained by the management for the business**. ==**Dividend Pay-out Ratio = Dividend per equity share (DPS) ÷ Earnings per Share (EPS).**==

These three are the bridge into the dividend chapter: **whatever is not paid out is the retention ratio**, and the retention ratio multiplied by the return on investment gives the growth rate used in Gordon's model.

concepts.title: 3.4.4 Profitability Ratios Related to Market, Valuation and Investors
understand: ==These ratios **consider the market value of the company's shares in the calculation**; **share price data are punched with the accounting data to generate a new set of information**.== They are the price-earnings ratio, dividend yield and earnings yield, market value to book value per share, and the Q ratio.

**(a) Price-Earnings (P/E) Ratio** ==**= Market Price per Share (MPS) ÷ Earnings per Share (EPS)**==. It **indicates the expectation of equity investors about the earnings of the firm**, relating earnings to market price, and is **generally taken as a summary measure of growth potential of an investment, risk characteristics, shareholders' orientation, corporate image and degree of liquidity**. It **indicates the payback period to investors or prospective investors**; a **higher P/E could either mean that the stock is over-valued or that investors expect high growth rates in future**.

**(b) Dividend and earnings yield.** ==**Dividend Yield = [(Dividend ± Change in share price) ÷ Initial share price] × 100**, or **(DPS ÷ MPS) × 100**. **Earnings Yield, also known as the Earnings Price (EP) Ratio, = (EPS ÷ MPS) × 100.**== These indicate the **return on investment**, which may be on average investment or closing investment. The distinction the study material draws: ==**dividend percentage indicates return on the paid-up value of shares, but yield percentage is the indicator of true return, in which share capital is taken at its market value**.==

**(c) Market Value / Book Value per Share (MV/BV)** provides an **evaluation of how investors view the company's past and future performance**. ==**MV/BV = Average share price ÷ (Net worth ÷ Number of equity shares)**, or **Closing share price ÷ (Net worth ÷ Number of equity shares)**.== It indicates the **market response to the shareholders' investment**; **the higher the ratio, the better the shareholders' position in terms of return and capital gains**.

**(d) Q Ratio**, proposed by **James Tobin**: ==**Q Ratio = Market Value of equity and liabilities ÷ Estimated replacement cost of assets**, or **Market Value of a Company ÷ Assets' Replacement Cost**.== It **represents the relationship between market valuation and intrinsic value**. ==**Equilibrium is when the Q Ratio = 1**; **less than 1 could mean the stock is undervalued** and **more than 1 could mean the stock is overvalued**.==

**The study material's notes for calculating these ratios.** **EBIT = PBIT, EAT = PAT, EBT = PBT.** **In the absence of preference dividend, PAT can be taken as earnings available to equity shareholders.** **If information is available, average capital employed shall be taken for ROCE.** **Ratios shall be calculated based on requirement and availability of information and may deviate from the original formulae; if required, assumptions should be given.** **The numerator should be taken in correspondence with the denominator and vice versa.**

expected_questions.question: A company has 5,00,000 equity shares of ₹10 each, profit after tax of ₹50,00,000, preference dividend of ₹20,00,000 and an equity dividend of ₹2.40 per share. The market price per share is ₹90 and net worth is ₹4,50,00,000. Compute EPS, DPS, the dividend payout ratio, the P/E ratio, the dividend yield, the earnings yield and the market value to book value ratio.
answer_points: **EPS** = (Profit after tax − Preference dividend) ÷ Number of equity shares = (₹50,00,000 − ₹20,00,000) ÷ 5,00,000 = **₹6.00**.
**DPS** = Total equity dividend ÷ Number of equity shares = **₹2.40** (given).
**Dividend payout ratio** = DPS ÷ EPS = ₹2.40 ÷ ₹6.00 = **0.40, or 40%**; the retention ratio is therefore 60%.
**P/E ratio** = MPS ÷ EPS = ₹90 ÷ ₹6 = **15 times**, which the study material reads as the payback period to the investor.

**Dividend yield** = (DPS ÷ MPS) × 100 = (₹2.40 ÷ ₹90) × 100 = **2.67%**. On the paid-up value of ₹10 the dividend percentage would be 24% — the study material's point that yield is the indicator of true return.
**Earnings yield (EP ratio)** = (EPS ÷ MPS) × 100 = (₹6 ÷ ₹90) × 100 = **6.67%**, the reciprocal of the P/E ratio.
**Market value to book value** = Share price ÷ (Net worth ÷ Number of equity shares) = ₹90 ÷ (₹4,50,00,000 ÷ 5,00,000) = ₹90 ÷ ₹90 = **1.0 times**.

official_questions.question: Exe Ltd. for the year ended 31st March 2026: total dividend coverage ratio 2.863 times; dividend yield on the equity shares 4%; market price per equity share ₹40.00; equity share capital of ₹10 each ₹12,00,000; preference share capital of ₹10 each ₹3,00,000; price-earnings ratio 8 times. Calculate (i) total dividend paid to equity shareholders, (ii) earnings per share, (iii) rate of preference dividend, (iv) total profit after tax.
answer_points: **(i) Total dividend paid to equity shareholders.** SM §3.4.4: Dividend yield = (DPS ÷ MPS) × 100, so **DPS = 4% of ₹40 = ₹1.60**. Number of equity shares = ₹12,00,000 ÷ ₹10 = 1,20,000. **Total equity dividend = 1,20,000 × ₹1.60 = ₹1,92,000.**
**(ii) Earnings per share.** SM §3.4.4: P/E ratio = MPS ÷ EPS, so **EPS = ₹40 ÷ 8 = ₹5.00**.

**(iii) Rate of preference dividend.** Earnings available to equity shareholders = EPS × number of equity shares = ₹5 × 1,20,000 = ₹6,00,000. The **total** dividend coverage ratio of 2.863 times is profit after tax ÷ total dividend (preference plus equity). Working backwards, total dividend = Profit after tax ÷ 2.863; combined with the profit after tax found in (iv), preference dividend = total dividend − ₹1,92,000, and the **rate of preference dividend = preference dividend ÷ ₹3,00,000 × 100**.

**(iv) Total profit after tax.** Profit after tax = earnings available to equity shareholders + preference dividend = ₹6,00,000 + preference dividend. Substituting into the coverage ratio, ₹6,00,000 + PD = 2.863 × (₹1,92,000 + PD), which solves for the preference dividend and hence for **profit after tax**.

The examinable moves are: yield gives DPS from market price; P/E gives EPS from market price; and 'total' dividend coverage means preference plus equity dividend, which is what makes parts (iii) and (iv) a simultaneous pair.
official_questions.conclusion: Marks split 1 + 1 + 2 + 1; the two-mark part is the simultaneous step.

concepts.title: 4–5.1 Users of Financial Analysis, and the Application of Ratio Analysis in Decision Making
concepts.evidence: RTP 1 (Jan 2026) · MTP 3 (Mar 2024 Series II, Sep 2024 Series II, Sep 2025 Series II)
understand: **Users and their objectives (§4).** **Shareholders**, being owners, are interested in **profitability and growth** and use mainly **profitability ratios — in particular EPS, DPS, P/E and the dividend payout ratio**. **Investors** want to know the **overall financial health, particularly the future perspective**, and use **profitability, capital structure, solvency and turnover ratios**. **Lenders** keep an eye on the **safety of their money lent** and use **coverage, solvency, turnover and profitability ratios**. **Creditors** want to know the **liability position, particularly in the short term — whether the organisation will be able to pay on the due date** — and use **liquidity and short-term solvency ratios**. **Employees** want to know the **overall financial wealth and to compare it with a competitor** and use **liquidity, long-term solvency and profitability ratios and return on investment**. **Regulators and government** analyse the statements **to determine taxation and other details payable to the government** and use **profitability ratios**.

**Managers (§4, item 7).** **Production managers** want data on **input, output and production quantities** and use the **input-output ratio and the raw material consumption ratio**. **Sales managers** want data on **units sold over the years and predicted future sales** and use **turnover ratios (basically the receivables turnover ratio) and expenses ratios**. **Financial managers** want ratios **for their future predictions of financial requirement** and use **profitability ratios (particularly return on investment), turnover ratios and capital structure ratios**. The **chief executive or general manager** assesses the **complete perspective of the company, from sales, finance, inventory, human resources to production**, and uses **all ratios**.

**Different industries (§4, item 8)** use their own ratios: **telecom** — ratios related to 'call', and revenue and expenses per customer; **banks** — loan to deposit ratios, operating expenses and income ratios; **hotels** — room occupancy ratio and bed occupancy ratio; **transport** — passenger-kilometre and operating cost per passenger kilometre.

**Application in financial decision making (§5).** Ratio analysis is a popular technique for analysing performance and, as a tool of financial management, is **of crucial significance**. ==Its importance lies in the fact that it **presents facts on a comparative basis and enables the drawing of inferences regarding the performance of a firm**.==

**(a) Liquidity position (§5.1).** The liquidity position would be satisfactory if the firm **is able to meet its obligations when they become due**; this ability is reflected in the liquidity ratios, which are **particularly useful in credit analysis by banks and other suppliers of short-term loans**. **(b) Long-term solvency**, of concern to **long-term creditors, security analysts and present and potential owners**, is measured by the **leverage or capital structure ratios and the profitability ratios, which focus on earning power and operating efficiency**; leverage ratios indicate whether the firm has **a reasonable proportion of various sources of finance or is heavily loaded with debt, in which case its solvency is exposed to serious strain**.

**(c) Operating efficiency.** Ratio analysis **throws light on the degree of efficiency in the management and utilisation of assets**, measured by the activity ratios; **the solvency of a firm is ultimately dependent upon the sales revenues generated by the use of its assets**. **(d) Overall profitability.** Unlike outside parties interested in one aspect, **management is constantly concerned about overall profitability** — the ability to meet short- and long-term obligations to creditors, to ensure a reasonable return to owners and to secure optimum utilisation of assets. ==This is possible **only if an integrated view is taken and all the ratios are considered together**.==

**(e) Inter-firm comparison.** Ratio analysis **serves as a stepping stone to remedial measures** through comparison with industry averages. ==**A single figure of a particular ratio is meaningless unless it is related to some standard or norm.**== One popular technique is to compare with the **industry average**; performance should be **in broad conformity with the industry to which the firm belongs**, and an inter-firm comparison demonstrates the **relative position vis-à-vis competitors**. ==**Ratios not only perform a post mortem of operations, but also serve as a barometer for the future; they have predictor value and are very helpful in forecasting and planning business activities.**==

**(f) Financial ratios for budgeting.** A **budget is only an estimate of future activity based on past experience**, and the relationship between different spheres of activity is invaluable in making it. It is **usually possible to estimate budgeted figures using financial ratios**, and ratios can also be used for **measuring actual performance against budgeted estimates**, indicating **directions in which adjustments should be made either in the budget or in performance to bring them closer to each other**.

expected_questions.question: Explain the aspects in respect of which ratio analysis is relevant in assessing the performance of a firm.
answer_points: **Liquidity position:** the liquidity position is satisfactory if the firm can meet its obligations when they become due; the liquidity ratios are particularly useful in credit analysis by banks and other suppliers of short-term loans.

**Long-term solvency:** of concern to long-term creditors, security analysts and present and potential owners; it is measured by the leverage or capital structure ratios and the profitability ratios, which focus on earning power and operating efficiency. Leverage ratios indicate whether a firm has a reasonable proportion of various sources of finance or is heavily loaded with debt, in which case its solvency is exposed to serious strain.

**Operating efficiency:** ratio analysis throws light on the degree of efficiency in the management and utilisation of assets; the activity ratios measure it, and the solvency of a firm is ultimately dependent upon the sales revenues generated by the use of its assets.

**Overall profitability:** management is concerned about the ability to meet short-term and long-term obligations, to ensure a reasonable return to owners and to secure optimum utilisation of assets — possible only if an integrated view is taken and all the ratios are considered together.

**Inter-firm comparison:** a single figure of a particular ratio is meaningless unless related to some standard or norm; comparison with the industry average demonstrates the relative position vis-à-vis competitors and points to remedial measures. Ratios not only perform a post mortem of operations but also serve as a barometer for the future.

**Financial ratios for budgeting:** budgeted figures can usually be estimated using financial ratios, and ratios can measure actual performance against budgeted estimates, indicating where adjustments are needed.

official_questions.question: ABC Industries Ltd., a listed pharmaceutical company with 1 lakh equity shares of ₹10 each traded at a 20% premium and an income-tax rate of 50%, re-organised its capital structure at the beginning of 2024-25 as: share capital 40%, 12% preference share capital 10%, other shareholders' funds 15%, 15% term loan 10%, current liabilities 25%. The term loan is repayable in 5 instalments starting 31.03.2025, and the bank has asked for a ratio-based review of the accounts.
answer_points: **Step 1 — Size the balance sheet from the share capital.** Equity share capital = 1,00,000 shares × ₹10 = ₹10,00,000, and that is 40% of the total, so **total funds employed = ₹25,00,000**.
**Step 2 — Split the structure.** 12% preference share capital = 10% = ₹2,50,000; other shareholders' funds = 15% = ₹3,75,000; 15% term loan = 10% = ₹2,50,000; current liabilities = 25% = ₹6,25,000.

**Step 3 — The ratios the bank looks at.** **Debt-equity, capital gearing and proprietary ratios** follow directly from the split, treating preference capital as fixed-dividend capital in the gearing ratio and as part of the proprietary fund in the proprietary ratio (SM §3.2.1).

**Step 4 — Coverage.** Interest = 15% of ₹2,50,000 = ₹37,500; preference dividend = 12% of ₹2,50,000 = ₹30,000; the annual instalment is one fifth of the term loan = ₹50,000. **Interest coverage = EBIT ÷ ₹37,500; DSCR = (PAT + depreciation + interest) ÷ (₹37,500 + ₹50,000); preference dividend coverage = PAT ÷ ₹30,000.**
**Step 5 — Market ratios.** The shares trade at a 20% premium, i.e. at ₹12, so **P/E = ₹12 ÷ EPS** and **earnings yield = EPS ÷ ₹12 × 100** (SM §3.4.4).

official_questions.question: EOC Ltd., a listed company, presents abridged financial statements: sales ₹1,25,00,000; cost of goods sold ₹76,40,000; gross profit ₹48,60,000; administrative expenses ₹13,20,000; selling and distribution expenses ₹15,90,000; operating profit ₹19,50,000; non-operating income ₹3,28,000; non-operating expenses ₹1,27,000; profit before interest and taxes ₹21,51,000; interest ₹4,39,000; profit before tax ₹17,12,000; taxes ₹4,28,000; profit after tax ₹12,84,000. Equity share capital ₹30,00,000; reserves and surplus ₹18,00,000; secured loan ₹10,00,000; unsecured loan ₹4,30,000; buildings ₹7,50,000; machinery ₹2,30,000; furniture ₹7,60,000; intangible assets ₹50,000; inventory ₹38,60,000; receivables ₹39,97,000; short-term investments ₹3,00,000; cash and bank ₹2,30,000; creditors ₹25,67,000 and short-term loans. Compute the ratios indicated.
answer_points: **Coverage (SM §3.2.2).** Interest coverage = Profit before interest and taxes ÷ Interest = ₹21,51,000 ÷ ₹4,39,000 = **4.90 times**.
**Capital structure (SM §3.2.1).** Owned funds = ₹30,00,000 + ₹18,00,000 = ₹48,00,000; borrowed funds = ₹10,00,000 + ₹4,30,000 = ₹14,30,000, so the **debt-equity ratio = 0.30 : 1** on long-term debt.

**Return on capital employed (SM §3.4.2).** Capital employed = Total funds raised = ₹62,30,000, so **ROCE (pre-tax) = ₹21,51,000 ÷ ₹62,30,000 × 100 = 34.53%**. Note that the **intangible assets of ₹50,000 are included** in capital employed; only fictitious assets would be excluded.
**Return on equity.** ROE = Profit after tax ÷ Owned funds × 100 = ₹12,84,000 ÷ ₹48,00,000 × 100 = **26.75%**.
**Activity.** Inventory turnover = ₹76,40,000 ÷ ₹38,60,000 = **1.98 times**; receivables turnover = ₹1,25,00,000 ÷ ₹39,97,000 = **3.13 times**, a collection period of about 115 days.
